clause: MUST establish accessibility requirements during design, alongside any other requirement
MUST verify conformance against WCAG 2.2 AA before a change reaches users
MUST assess third-party components against WCAG 2.2 AA before we adopt them, and record what falls short
MUST publish an accessibility statement where we are required to, and keep it truthful about the gaps that remain
MUST NOT ship a change that knowingly makes accessibility worse without a recorded deviation (pol-DEVI) and a plan to correct it
SHOULD test with the assistive technologies people actually use, on the journeys that matter most
COULD involve disabled users in research and testing directly, rather than inferring their experience from a checklist
MUST grant access to a named individual or a distinctly identified workload, never to a shared persona
MUST grant the least privilege that allows the work to be done, and no more
MUST keep the ability to make a change separate from the ability to approve or release it. See pol-AGNT
MUST require strong authentication for access to our systems, our code and our data
MUST review access rights on a defined cycle, confirming each grant is still needed
MUST remove access promptly when a role changes or a person leaves
MUST control and record the use of privileged administrative tooling
MUST NOT operate shared or generic privileged accounts where individual attribution is lost. See pol-EVER
MUST NOT leave standing production access in place beyond what the role genuinely requires
SHOULD hold identity in a single directory, so that access granted or removed once takes effect everywhere
COULD hold no standing privilege at all, granting privileged access on request and only for as long as the work takes
MUST record where an agent-produced contribution came from, in enough detail that reviewing it is a check rather than an act of faith
MUST require a person to accept agent-produced work before it carries any authority, and that person owns it afterwards as if they had written it
MUST hold agent-produced changes to every gate that applies to our own: the same review, the same automated verification under pol-AUTV, the same route to production
MUST state how confident we are in an observation, and let unverified ones expire rather than stay on unchallenged
MUST NOT treat an agent's own account of its work as verification of that work
MUST NOT approve or merge an agent-authored change under the identity that opened or accepted it. See pol-ACCS
MUST NOT accept a proposal we cannot trace back to what produced it
MUST NOT grant an agent access, privilege or a route to production that an individual doing the same work would not be granted
MUST build and verify every change automatically, on integration, without anyone asking for it
MUST treat a failing check as blocking: a red build does not merge and does not promote
MUST be able to reproduce a build from version control alone, on any machine set up to do so
MUST test at the levels the change warrants, fast enough that the feedback arrives while the work is still in hand
MUST add a regression test for every defect we fix, so it can only be found once. See pol-VURM
MUST treat a broken default branch as the team's first priority
MUST NOT merge or release over a failing check without a recorded deviation (pol-DEVI)
MUST NOT disable, skip, silence or suppress a check or a warning without a recorded deviation (pol-DEVI)
MUST NOT depend on a particular person's machine to produce a build
SHOULD integrate to the default branch often enough that any one change is small enough to reason about
SHOULD treat a new warning as a defect to triage rather than noise to accumulate
SHOULD know what proportion of our code the tests exercise, and notice when it falls
COULD produce byte-for-byte identical output from the same source
MUST attribute the running cost of a system to the service and the team that owns it
MUST give the people who own a system visibility of what it costs, at a cadence that lets them act
MUST state expected running cost as a design output for new systems and significant changes
MUST size resources against what they actually use, and revisit that as usage changes
MUST notice unexpected cost quickly, and investigate a sharp unexplained rise
MUST remove what we no longer use, including in environments below production
MUST NOT run a production workload that nobody owns the cost of
MUST NOT let cost efficiency erode resilience, security or accessibility
MUST classify data by sensitivity and handle each class according to that classification
MUST protect sensitive data in transit and at rest using current, well-regarded cryptographic algorithms
MUST retire a cryptographic algorithm as it weakens
MUST handle personal data on a lawful basis
MUST collect only the personal data that is needed
MUST support the rights of the people the data concerns
MUST know where our sensitive and personal data lives
MUST hold and process personal data only where a lawful transfer mechanism covers it
MUST delete data when its defined retention period ends
MUST NOT place unmasked production or personal data into an environment below production. See pol-ENVS
MUST NOT send personal data to a third party before a written processing agreement covers it
MUST NOT retain sensitive or personal data beyond its defined lifetime without a recorded deviation (pol-DEVI)
MUST NOT write unmasked sensitive personal data into logs or telemetry. See pol-SCRT
COULD change cryptographic algorithm without re-architecting what depends on it, rather than treating the choice as permanent
COULD protect sensitive data so that it is never processed in the clear
MUST state what a correct output looks like, in terms that can be checked automatically
MUST check a production output against those expectations before anything downstream uses it
MUST keep, for each production run, a record of its inputs, its output and its check result
MUST NOT use a derived output whose checks did not pass
SHOULD be able to trace a derived value back through the runs that produced it to its source
MUST record a deviation before departing from a policy or standard, or immediately afterwards where an incident left no time
MUST name an individual who accepts the risk: someone with the authority to accept it, never a team or a role in the abstract
MUST state what the deviation is, why it is needed and what compensates for it
MUST give every deviation a review date
MUST make deviations visible to those affected by the risk, rather than filing them where only the person who raised them will look
MUST close a deviation by fixing the underlying gap or by consciously re-accepting the risk, with the same scrutiny as the first time
MUST NOT treat a deviation as permanent by default, or let an expired one stand unreviewed
MUST NOT treat a long-standing practice as exempt from a policy it breaks
SHOULD record a shortcut taken knowingly, so that it is tracked work rather than something the next person discovers
MUST separate production from non-production, with distinct access controls at each tier
MUST keep production credentials and secrets unreachable from any lower environment. See pol-SCRT
MUST provision environments from the same definitions, so that what passes below production is a fair test of what will run in it
MUST be able to state the configuration an environment is running, and reproduce it
MUST promote changes between environments through automation rather than by manual copy
MUST mask or synthesise the data used below production
MUST NOT develop, test or debug against the live production system
MUST NOT reuse a production secret in any environment below production. See pol-SCRT
MUST NOT place unmasked production or personal data into a lower environment. See pol-DATA
SHOULD be able to create an environment on demand and discard it when the work is done
MUST hold every asset needed to build, deploy, run and recover a solution in version control
MUST preserve a complete change history that attributes each change to an individual
MUST link each change to the work that asked for it
MUST protect the default branch, so changes arrive by reviewed merge rather than direct push
MUST subject changes to infrastructure, schema and configuration to the same review as changes to application code
MUST NOT allow an asset that is necessary to reproduce a system to exist only on an individual's machine, in a console, or in a shared drive
MUST NOT accept shared or generic accounts that make a change unattributable. See pol-ACCS
COULD prove the authorship of a change cryptographically, rather than trusting what it claims
MUST maintain a defined incident-response process with clear roles, so that during an incident it is never ambiguous who decides
MUST classify incidents by severity, and escalate according to it
MUST communicate an incident's status to those it affects, at the cadence its severity sets
MUST invoke the recovery path defined for the affected system rather than improvising one
MUST preserve evidence and produce a record for every significant incident, and for every personal data breach whether or not it is notifiable
MUST notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach within the statutory window
MUST tell the people a personal data breach puts at high risk, without undue delay
MUST encourage anyone to report a suspected incident, and make it easy to do so
MUST review significant incidents afterwards, looking for the conditions that allowed them rather than for someone to blame
MUST turn the findings of those reviews into tracked work. See pol-SECD
MUST rehearse the process rather than first exercising it for real
MUST NOT handle a significant incident informally, with no record and no named owner
MUST NOT close an incident before the learning from it is captured
MUST define each interface against an explicit, documented contract, and treat that contract as the source of truth rather than the implementation
MUST version interfaces so that a change we need does not become a break others must absorb
MUST publish a deprecation approach, saying how much notice a consumer gets
MUST give notice before removing or changing something consumers depend on
MUST secure interfaces by default: authenticated, authorised, and validating what they are given
MUST verify our contracts hold, rather than trusting that they do
MUST NOT make a breaking change to a published interface without a version increment and notice to its consumers
MUST NOT expose sensitive data or a sensitive operation through an unauthenticated interface
MUST document what is needed to build, run and recover each solution, and version that documentation
MUST change documentation alongside the code, configuration or process it describes, in the same review
MUST record architecturally significant decisions, with the reasoning and the alternatives weighed, so a future reader can tell a considered choice from an accident
MUST document the rules we expect agent-produced work to follow, where the agents doing that work will read them (pol-AGNT)
MUST NOT allow knowledge that is critical to operating or recovering a system to exist only in someone's head or in an ephemeral conversation
MUST NOT maintain a separate copy of documentation for agents to read
MUST segment by trust boundary and by environment
MUST deny by default, and expose a service only through an intended, controlled route
MUST protect traffic crossing a trust boundary
MUST verify the identity presented at the far end of a connection that crosses a trust boundary, and refuse it where that fails
MUST prefer private paths to public ones for access between our own services
MUST control what leaves our systems, not only what arrives
MUST define network topology as reviewable code, under pol-EVER
MUST NOT expose a management interface or a datastore directly to the public internet
MUST NOT leave traffic between our own systems unrestricted where they have no need to talk to each other
MUST NOT disable, bypass or weaken identity verification at a trust boundary
COULD authenticate and authorise every service-to-service call, so that network location grants no trust
MUST emit operational and security-relevant telemetry to a central store that the emitting system cannot alter or delete
MUST keep timestamps consistent across systems, so events can be correlated into one timeline
MUST retain telemetry for a defined period: long enough to investigate, no longer than justified
MUST monitor the availability and health of production systems, and alert an accountable owner when they degrade
MUST monitor for security-relevant events, not only for availability
MUST treat alerts as something to be acted on, and keep them few enough and meaningful enough that they still are
MUST NOT run a production system with no monitoring and no alerting
MUST NOT write secrets, credentials or unmasked sensitive personal data into telemetry. See pol-SCRT and pol-DATA
SHOULD express what good looks like as service-level objectives, and monitor against them
SHOULD emit telemetry that can be correlated across systems by a shared identifier, not only by time
MUST state performance and capacity targets for systems where performance matters, in terms that can be measured
MUST validate against those targets before significant releases, under conditions representative of real load rather than convenient load
MUST treat a target we no longer meet as a defect, not as a new baseline
MUST understand behaviour at peak and over time, not only at the average case on a quiet afternoon
MUST NOT release a significant change to a performance-sensitive system with no performance validation at all
MUST deploy to production only through an automated pipeline
MUST promote one artefact through the environments rather than rebuilding it for each stage
MUST hold environment-specific configuration outside the artefact, so the artefact promoted between environments is the one that was built
MUST be able to trace any production release to the change, the artefact and the approval behind it. See pol-TRUS
MUST have a defined rollback or recovery path before a change goes to production
MUST hold the pipeline itself in version control under pol-EVER, as a reviewed artefact like any other
MUST carry the safeguards that change approval exists to provide inside the pipeline, rather than treating automation as a reason to drop them
MUST treat a flag that changes production behaviour as a controlled, auditable change
MUST NOT hand-edit production, whether code, configuration, infrastructure or schema, other than a flag change made under FLAGS
MUST NOT deploy an artefact built outside the pipeline
COULD release progressively, promoting or reversing on live signals rather than on a decision made beforehand
MUST define recovery-time and recovery-point objectives for critical systems, and design to meet them
MUST back up critical data on a schedule that matches those objectives
MUST test restoration periodically
MUST keep at least one copy of critical data outside the failure domain of its source
MUST bound every outbound call in time, so a slow dependency cannot become an unbounded wait
MUST design so that the failure of one dependency degrades function rather than taking the system down with it
MUST make operations that may be retried safe to re-run
MUST NOT rely on a backup that has never been test-restored
MUST NOT retry indefinitely, without limit or backoff, against a failing dependency
SHOULD run critical services across more than one failure domain
SHOULD shed or slow work deliberately when load exceeds capacity, turning some requests away rather than failing unpredictably
COULD prove resilience by causing failure deliberately, rather than waiting to observe one
MUST hold secrets in a controlled store, with access granted by identity, restricted to those who need it, and recorded
MUST rotate any secret on a defined cycle and on any suspicion of compromise, without a code change
MUST protect the keys and certificates that protect our data through their full lifecycle: issue, storage, rotation, revocation
MUST actively look for secrets that have leaked into places they should never reach
MUST NOT commit a secret to version control, place one in a configuration file or pipeline definition, or bake one into a build artefact
MUST NOT use a production secret anywhere outside production. See pol-ENVS
MUST NOT write a secret to a log, a console, an error message or a support ticket. See pol-DATA
COULD reach a position where there is no static secret left to leak
MUST capture security and privacy requirements for new systems and features, as requirements rather than as afterthoughts
MUST apply established secure-design principles: least privilege, defence in depth, secure defaults, and failing closed so that a failure denies rather than allows
MUST think through how a significant new system or high-risk change could be attacked, and record what we found
MUST assess the impact on people before starting processing likely to be high risk to them
MUST turn the findings into tracked work rather than leaving them in a document. See pol-INCR
MUST write code to a documented secure-coding standard for the stack it is written in
MUST review code for security and correctness, not only for style
MUST NOT take a high-risk change into build with no security requirements and no consideration of threat
MUST maintain an inventory of what each solution depends on, naming each component and the version in use
MUST screen a component for known vulnerabilities before we adopt it
MUST screen a component's licence for terms we cannot accept before we adopt it
MUST scan the artefacts we build for malicious content before we release them
MUST obtain components from sources we have reason to trust
MUST establish which security responsibilities we hold and which the provider holds, before adopting a service
MUST know how we would leave a service before we depend on it
MUST hold build artefacts in a managed repository, versioned and retained so a release can be identified, rolled back and examined later
MUST be able to trace a deployed artefact to the change and the build that produced it. See pol-PIPE
MUST review the components and services we depend on periodically, not only when we adopt them
MUST NOT introduce a component or artefact from an untrusted or unverifiable source
MUST NOT alter a released artefact in place
SHOULD refuse into production any artefact whose origin cannot be cryptographically proven
MUST actively look for vulnerabilities across the whole stack, through the lifecycle rather than only at release
MUST prioritise findings by severity and by how exploitable they actually are, not by which tool reported them
MUST set remediation timeframes by severity, and track findings to closure against them
MUST provide a route for people outside the organisation to report a vulnerability to us, and respond when they do
MUST keep a regression test for a vulnerability we have fixed, so it cannot return unnoticed. See pol-AUTV
MUST NOT release with an unremediated critical finding absent a recorded, risk-owned deviation (pol-DEVI)
MUST NOT leave a critical, exploitable vulnerability past its remediation timeframe with nobody accountable for it
SHOULD have significant or externally-exposed systems tested by people who did not build them
